guideTitle: Best Electric Space Heaters for RVs (2026)
metaTitle: Best Electric Space Heaters for RVs 2026
metaDescription: Six electric heaters for RVs compared across portable, wall-mount and low-profile designs, with notes on amp draw, mounting and safety shutoffs.
expertTake: The Xtreme Heaters 600/1200W is the best electric pick for a typical RV because it was built for cabins and its wattage steps respect a 30 amp service. The Suburban wall unit is the value-minded install, and anyone who lives on a pedestal with spare capacity can simply buy a standard 1500 watt DREO.
introParagraphs: Electric heaters turn watts into warmth at close to full efficiency, so the real choice is not how much warmth you get but how it arrives. Some blow it with a fan, some radiate it from a panel, and some sit on a wall so they take no floor space at all.

An RV changes the priorities. Floor space is scarce, the electrical service is limited, and the floor moves while you drive. The best electric unit here is the one that fits the room you have and the amps you can spare.

products.name: Xtreme Heaters 600/1200W Boat Cabin RV Heater
products.description:
Xtreme Heaters designed this unit for boats, cabins and RVs, and the engineering shows in two places. The air intake sits on top, so you can slide the back flush against a wall or cabinet without starving the fan. The base is wide and low, which resists tipping when a rig shifts.

Its two power steps, 600 and 1200 watts, are chosen with small electrical systems in mind. At 1200 watts it pulls about 10 amps, leaving two or more amps of headroom compared with a 1500 watt heater on the same circuit. Against the DREO portable in this roundup it offers less peak heat but a more forgiving load.

Keep it away from bedding and curtains and wipe the top intake monthly. A tip-over switch is part of the design, so test it once at the start of each season. Pack it upright in a cabinet for travel, ideally wedged with a towel so it cannot slide when the rig brakes hard.
products.bestFor: 30 amp RV owners who want a purpose-built, low-draw heater.
pros: Top intake lets it sit against a wall
1200W peak draws about 10 amps

Made for boats and RVs, not offices
cons: Lower peak heat than a 1500W unit
Less known brand than the big names

products.name: Suburban 2691ABK Slim Wall-Mount RV Electric Heater
products.description:
Suburban's 2691ABK is a fixed, thin electric heater meant to be screwed to the wall of an RV. Because it is under five inches thick, it protrudes less than most hallway features, and it takes zero floor space. The adjustable thermostat and variable heat settings let you set it once and leave it.

A fixed heater cannot slide off a shelf or fall during a turn, which removes the tip-over problem entirely. The trade is flexibility: it lives where you bolt it and heats the zone around that spot. Next to the portable DREO, it is quieter in daily life but demands a few minutes with a stud finder and screws.

RV-specific brands like Suburban also publish clear installation steps, which helps when wiring to a dedicated circuit. Check the wall for water lines or wiring before you drill, and use the studs or a backing plate rather than thin paneling alone, since the weight and the vibration of the road work on those screws constantly. If the unit is hardwired, have the connection checked by someone competent.
products.bestFor: Owners who want a permanent, floor-free heater in one zone.
pros: Wall mount frees all floor space
Under 5 inches thick, discreet profile
Fixed mount cannot tip over in transit
Adjustable thermostat holds a set temperature
cons: Fixed in one spot, so zone heat only
Needs mounting and possibly wiring work
Not portable between rooms or rigs

products.name: DREO 1500W Portable Heater with Remote and 12H Timer
products.description:
DREO's portable fan heater pairs a 1500 watt PTC element with an NTC temperature chipset for steadier regulation. The remote and 12 hour timer make it easy to schedule warmth before you wake, and five modes let you choose between full power and a gentler setting.

It is the strongest portable heater here, delivering the full 5,100 BTU an electric element can at 1500 watts. That also means about 12.5 amps on high, which can trip a shared 30 amp breaker in an RV with the air conditioner on. The Xtreme draws less, so the DREO fits best when you have spare capacity.

Because it stands on the floor, store it in a bin and pad it for travel. A dusty intake raises fan noise, so vacuum the grille monthly. The timer is helpful but should never replace common sense about leaving a heater alone.
products.bestFor: Pedestal campers with spare amps who want strong portable heat.
pros: 1500W delivers the maximum from a plug-in heater
Remote and 12H timer suit bedtime use
NTC chipset gives tighter temperature control
Multiple modes let you trim output
cons: Full 12.5 amp draw strains a shared circuit
Floor unit needs stowing for travel
Fan noise rises as dust builds up

products.name: DREO Smart Wall Heater with Alexa and IP24 Rating
products.description:
This DREO is a wall-mounted PTC heater with an ALCI-style plug and an IP24 rating, meaning it resists splashing water. That splash resistance is useful in an RV bathroom or kitchenette, where steam and drips are common. Remote, app and Alexa voice control make it a smart option.

PTC heating with optimized airflow warms the zone quickly, and an ECO mode holds the temperature you choose. Against the Suburban slim wall unit, it adds smart features and bathroom suitability but has less RV-specific heritage. Both mount to the wall, so you give up portability.

Wall mounting also frees the floor and cuts tip-over risk. Confirm the rating suits your use before installing near a shower. Keep the intake clear of towels, and check the plug and cord periodically.
products.bestFor: Bathrooms and kitchenettes where splash resistance helps.
pros: IP24 rating tolerates splashes in a bathroom
Wall mount keeps the floor clear
Remote, app and Alexa control options
ECO mode regulates temperature
cons: Smart features need Wi-Fi and a phone

products.name: Heat Storm HS-1500-PHX-WIFI Wall Infrared Heater
products.description:
Heat Storm's HS-1500-PHX-WIFI is a radiant panel that hangs on the wall, with a touch screen and Wi-Fi control. Infrared heat warms objects and people in its line of sight, so you feel it directly rather than waiting for the air to heat. It is silent, since there is no fan.

A radiant panel suits a seating area or a bed wall, where you want direct warmth without moving air. It is not the best choice for heating a whole closed cabin quickly, which is where a fan heater like the DREO shines. The Wi-Fi app lets you adjust it from your phone.

Panels draw up to 1500 watts, so plan the circuit like any other heater. Mount it away from curtains and keep the surface clear. Check the wall bracket for tightness after a long drive.
products.bestFor: Quiet radiant warmth aimed at a seating or sleeping area.
pros: Silent radiant heat with no fan noise
Wall mount saves floor space
Touch screen and Wi-Fi app control
Tip-over shutoff and remote included
cons: Warms what it faces, not the whole air volume

products.name: GiveBest 1500W/750W Ceramic Desk Heater with Thermostat
products.description:
GiveBest sells a compact ceramic heater with 1500 and 750 watt steps, a thermostat and a cool-air fan mode. The built-in carry handle is practical for moving it between a bedroom and a dinette. Flame-retardant housing and automatic cutoffs are part of the listing.

It sits on the lower end of the price tier, so it is the one to buy if you want basic electric heat without extras. Its 750 watt step is a fair match for a shared RV circuit, and the 1500 watt step handles cold mornings. Against the Xtreme, it has a more office-like design and no RV-specific features.

Being compact, it fits a cupboard. Keep the cord away from the fan and avoid placing it on soft surfaces. Wipe the front grille now and then to keep the airflow clear.
products.bestFor: Budget shoppers who want simple portable heat.
pros: Two power steps plus fan-only mode
Carry handle makes it easy to move

cons: Fan is louder than the premium units

buyingCriteria.explanation: A 30 amp RV service gives you about 3,600 watts across everything. A 1500 watt heater uses about 12.5 amps, which leaves little for the air conditioner or microwave. The Xtreme at 1200 watts draws about 10 amps and the GiveBest at 750 watts draws about 6. Match the heater to the amps you actually have, and count the water heater element and the converter charging load too, because those quietly use part of the same budget.

A fixed wall unit like the Suburban or the DREO wall heater cannot tip over and takes no floor space. A portable one lets you move heat where you need it. The right answer depends on whether you want a set-and-forget zone or a flexible tool.

Fan heaters warm the air quickly and fill a small cabin, while radiant panels like the Heat Storm warm the surfaces and people in front of them. Radiant is silent, but fan heat reaches more of the room. In a tiny RV, a fan heater is usually faster, but a radiant panel makes sense over a dinette where people sit still for an hour at a time.

Bathrooms and kitchenettes bring steam and splashes. The DREO wall heater lists an IP24 rating, which means it resists splashing, while most portable units do not. Never use a standard heater in a wet area unless it is labeled for it.

A heater on an RV floor will slide and tip. Tip-over switches and overheat cutoffs are standard on good models, and the Xtreme adds a low, wide base. Verify these are listed before buying and look for UL or ETL marks. A heater without them is a poor bet in any rig, whatever its price.

A remote and timer, as on the DREO portable, help at bedtime. A touch screen and Wi-Fi on the Heat Storm suit tech-friendly owners. If you will never use an app, do not pay for one. A plain thermostat dial on the GiveBest does the same job for many owners without needing a phone signal in a remote campground.

howWeEvaluated.title: Electrical fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared peak wattage against a 30 amp RV service. The Xtreme at 1200 watts and the GiveBest at 750 watts score best for sharing, while the 1500 watt units demand more headroom. We used the spec sheets for this.

howWeEvaluated.title: Mounting and stability
howWeEvaluated.description: We rated how each heater stays put on a moving rig. Fixed wall units earned top marks and low wide bases came next. Tall or narrow designs scored lower.

howWeEvaluated.title: Heat delivery
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared fan, ceramic and infrared delivery for small cabins. Fan units warm the air quickest, while radiant panels suit seating zones. Each pick was judged against the job it is meant for.

howWeEvaluated.title: Controls
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at thermostats, remotes, timers and apps. We favored controls that help overnight use and discounted features that need a phone. The DREO portable and Heat Storm lead here.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety listing
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked for UL or ETL language, tip-over shutoff and overheat cutoffs. Where a listing was silent, we did not assume the feature existed. Based on owner feedback patterns, plug warmth is the most common complaint.

cards.label: Portable
cards.text: The Xtreme, DREO and GiveBest move wherever you need heat and store away for summer. They take floor space and need securing when you drive.

cards.label: Wall-mounted
cards.text: The Suburban, DREO wall and Heat Storm free the floor and cannot tip. They heat one zone and need installation.

howToChoose.note: Full-timers benefit from wall units, while weekenders usually prefer portable heaters. If you rent the rig or plan to sell it, a portable unit leaves no screw holes behind.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Pick a lower wattage step and check the amp draw on the listing. Avoid running a heater with the air conditioner or a microwave on the same circuit.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Xtreme at 1200 watts and the GiveBest 750 watt step are the best fits. Use the DREO portable's lower modes if you already own one.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You live in the RV or want a permanent, quiet setup. The Suburban and Heat Storm earn their cost through mounting and silence.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You camp occasionally and need only a quick boost. The GiveBest or Xtreme covers it.

maintenance.why: Dust restricts airflow and adds fan noise. A vacuum brush clears it in a minute.
Heat discolors a bad connection first. Replace any heater with a warm plug.
Road vibration loosens screws over time. Tighten them before a long trip.
Tilting a running portable should cut power. It confirms the safety switch still works.
Dust and moisture can corrode contacts. A bag or box keeps it clean.

faq.q: Should I choose a portable or wall-mounted RV heater?
faq.a: Portable heaters give flexibility and are simple to use, while wall units save space and cannot tip. Choose wall-mounted if you live aboard and portable if you travel light.

faq.q: How much will an electric heater add to my electric bill?
faq.a: One hour at 1500 watts uses 1.5 kilowatt-hours, so cost depends on your rate. At a campground with metered power, a thermostat helps keep the figure down.

faq.q: Will it trip my RV breaker?
faq.a: It can when combined with an air conditioner or a microwave. A 1500 watt heater draws about 12.5 amps, so use a lower step when other loads are running.

faq.q: Is radiant heat more efficient than a fan heater?
faq.a: Both turn electricity into heat at about the same efficiency. Radiant panels feel warmer sooner when you sit in front of them, while fan heaters warm the air quicker.

faq.q: Can an electric heater replace the furnace?
faq.a: In mild weather yes, but in deep cold a furnace or diesel heater covers more space. Electric heaters work best as supplements or on shore power.

faq.q: Do I need an extension cord?
faq.a: No. Plug directly into a receptacle or pedestal outlet. Thin extension cords can overheat at heater loads, and a warm plug or cord end is the earliest warning sign that a connection is failing. Replace the cord or the heater instead of tolerating it.
